stem: A company just created its AWS account using a company email address. The root user has full access to everything.
prompt: What should the company do FIRST to protect the root user?

options.text: Share the root password with all administrators
options.why: Sharing root credentials increases risk.

options.text: Use the root user for daily tasks
options.why: Daily work should use less privileged identities.

options.text: Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the root user
options.why: MFA adds a second factor so a stolen password alone can't be used.

options.text: Create root user access keys for automation
options.why: Root access keys are risky and should not be created.

explanation.answer: Enable MFA on the root user, avoid using it for everyday tasks, and don't create root access keys.
explanation.concept: Use IAM Identity Center or IAM users and roles for daily administration.
explanation.examTip: Root user: MFA on, no access keys, lock it away.

stem: An administrator with full AdministratorAccess permissions cannot complete one task and is told it requires the root user.
prompt: Which task requires the root user?

options.text: Creating an S3 bucket
options.why: IAM identities with S3 permissions can create buckets.

options.text: Launching an EC2 instance
options.why: IAM identities with EC2 permissions can launch instances.

options.text: Creating a new IAM user
options.why: Administrators with IAM permissions can create users.

options.text: Closing the AWS account
options.why: Closing the account is one of the tasks that require root user credentials.

explanation.answer: Some tasks require the root user, such as closing the account, changing account settings like the root email, and restoring IAM administrator permissions.
explanation.concept: Keep root credentials safe and use them only for these tasks.
explanation.examTip: Close account, change root email, change support plan = root user tasks.

references.title: Tasks that require root user credentials

stem: A developer only needs to read objects from one S3 bucket.
prompt: Which permission approach follows AWS best practice?

options.text: Grant read access to that bucket only
options.why: Least privilege grants only the permissions required.

options.text: Attach AmazonS3FullAccess for convenience
options.why: Full S3 access exceeds what the developer needs.

options.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess policy
options.why: This grants far more access than needed.

options.text: Give the developer the root user password
options.why: Root credentials should never be shared.

explanation.answer: Least privilege means granting only the permissions needed to perform a task.
explanation.concept: Start with narrow permissions and expand only when necessary.
explanation.examTip: Only what's needed = least privilege.

stem: A company has 30 developers who all need the same permissions.
prompt: What is the EASIEST way to manage their permissions with IAM users?

options.text: Use the root user for all developers
options.why: Root credentials should never be shared.

options.text: Put the users in an IAM group and attach the policy to the group
options.why: Group policies apply to every member, so changes happen in one place.

options.text: Create one shared IAM user for all developers
options.why: Shared users remove individual accountability.

options.text: Attach the same policy to each user one by one
options.why: This works but is hard to maintain, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: IAM groups are collections of IAM users. Policies attached to a group apply to all its members.
explanation.concept: Groups simplify permission management; users can belong to multiple groups.
explanation.examTip: Same permissions for many users = IAM group.

stem: An application on an EC2 instance needs to write to an Amazon S3 bucket.
prompt: What is the MOST secure way to give it access?

options.text: Add a bucket policy allowing any principal to write
options.why: Allowing any principal exposes the bucket to everyone.

options.text: Store root user access keys on the instance
options.why: Root keys should never be created or used this way.

options.text: Attach an IAM role to the instance
options.why: Roles provide temporary credentials that rotate automatically.

options.text: Store an IAM user's access keys in the application's code
options.why: Hard-coded keys can leak and are hard to rotate.

explanation.answer: IAM roles give AWS services temporary credentials. An instance profile lets applications on EC2 use the role without stored keys.
explanation.concept: Prefer temporary credentials over long-term access keys.
explanation.examTip: AWS service needs permissions = IAM role (not access keys).

stem: A company wants to make sure a stolen password alone is not enough to sign in to its AWS accounts.

options.text: Password reuse across accounts
options.why: Reusing passwords increases risk, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Longer session timeouts
options.why: Longer sessions don't add a second factor.

options.text: Public access to S3 buckets
options.why: This is unrelated and reduces security, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
options.why: MFA requires a second factor, such as a code or security key, in addition to the password.

explanation.answer: MFA adds an extra layer of protection by requiring something you have, like a security key, in addition to something you know.
explanation.concept: AWS supports passkeys and security keys, virtual authenticator apps and hardware TOTP tokens.
explanation.examTip: Stolen password protection = MFA.

stem: A security engineer reviews an IAM policy written in JSON with Effect, Action and Resource elements.

options.text: Which actions are allowed or denied on which resources
options.why: IAM policies define permissions using Effect, Action and Resource.

options.text: Which Availability Zone hosts an instance
options.why: AZ placement isn't defined by IAM policies.

options.text: How much a service will cost
options.why: Policies define permissions, not pricing.

options.text: Which Region a resource is created in
options.why: Region placement is chosen when creating a resource, not in this way.

explanation.answer: IAM policies are JSON documents that define permissions: whether actions are allowed or denied on specific resources, optionally with conditions.
explanation.concept: Policies can be attached to users, groups and roles, or to resources (resource-based policies).
explanation.examTip: IAM policy = Effect + Action + Resource (+ Condition).

stem: A developer uses the AWS CLI from a laptop.
prompt: Which credential type does the CLI typically use for an IAM user?

options.text: An SSH key pair created for EC2
options.why: SSH keys are for logging in to instances, not for AWS API calls.

options.text: Access keys (key ID and secret access key)
options.why: Programmatic access uses access keys, ideally short-term ones.

options.text: A TLS certificate issued by AWS Certificate Manager
options.why: ACM certificates secure websites, not CLI sign-in.

options.text: The console password with an MFA code
options.why: The CLI doesn't sign requests with the console password.

explanation.answer: Access keys are used to sign programmatic requests from the AWS CLI or SDKs. AWS recommends temporary credentials, for example through IAM Identity Center.
explanation.concept: Rotate long-term keys regularly and never commit them to code repositories.
explanation.examTip: CLI/SDK = access keys (prefer temporary credentials).

references.title: Managing access keys for IAM users

stem: A company with 15 AWS accounts wants employees to sign in once with their corporate identities and access the accounts they need.

options.text: Amazon Cognito user pools for employees
options.why: Cognito is mainly for customer-facing application users.

options.text: Separate IAM users in each account
options.why: Managing users in 15 accounts is hard and lacks single sign-on.

options.text: AWS IAM Identity Center
options.why: Identity Center provides single sign-on to multiple accounts and can connect to a corporate identity provider.

options.text: AWS Directory Service only
options.why: A directory alone doesn't provide multi-account access management.

explanation.answer: AWS IAM Identity Center centrally manages workforce access to multiple AWS accounts and applications, with single sign-on.
explanation.concept: It can use its own directory or connect to providers like Microsoft Entra ID or Okta.
explanation.examTip: Employees + many accounts + single sign-on = IAM Identity Center.

stem: A mobile app needs sign-up and sign-in for millions of customers, including sign-in with social providers.
prompt: Which AWS service is designed for this?

options.text: IAM users for each customer
options.why: IAM users are for access to your AWS account, not app customers.

options.text: AWS IAM Identity Center
options.why: Identity Center manages workforce access to AWS accounts, not customer sign-in for apps.

options.text: AWS Organizations
options.why: Organizations manages AWS accounts, not app users.

options.text: Amazon Cognito
options.why: Cognito provides user sign-up, sign-in and access control for web and mobile apps.

explanation.answer: Amazon Cognito adds user sign-up, sign-in and social or enterprise federation to applications, scaling to millions of users.
explanation.concept: Identity Center = workforce. Cognito = customers of your app.
explanation.examTip: App customers signing in = Cognito.

stem: A company has many AWS accounts and wants to manage them centrally and apply policies across them.

options.text: AWS Organizations
options.why: Organizations lets you centrally manage accounts, group them into OUs and apply policies.

options.text: AWS Config
options.why: Config tracks resource configurations, not account management.

options.text: AWS Artifact
options.why: Artifact provides compliance reports, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: AWS Organizations helps you centrally govern multiple accounts with organizational units (OUs), policies and consolidated billing.
explanation.concept: Service control policies (SCPs) set permission guardrails across accounts.
explanation.examTip: Manage many accounts centrally = AWS Organizations.

stem: A company wants to prevent any user in its development accounts, including administrators, from using AWS Regions outside Europe.

options.text: Security groups that block European traffic
options.why: Security groups filter network traffic, not API calls to Regions.

options.text: Service control policies (SCPs)
options.why: SCPs set maximum permissions for accounts in an OU, even for administrators.

options.text: An IAM group with a deny policy in each account
options.why: Account administrators could change or bypass this.

options.text: AWS Budgets actions in each account
options.why: Budget actions react to cost thresholds; they don't enforce Region restrictions.

explanation.answer: SCPs define the maximum available permissions for member accounts. They can deny actions outside approved Regions.
explanation.concept: SCPs don't grant permissions; they only limit what IAM policies can allow.
explanation.examTip: Guardrails across accounts (even admins) = SCPs.

stem: An SCP attached to an OU allows only Amazon S3 actions. A user in a member account has an IAM policy that allows EC2 actions.

options.text: Use all AWS services, because SCPs grant permissions
options.why: SCPs never grant permissions, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Use EC2 and S3, because the IAM policy grants EC2
options.why: The SCP limits the account to S3 actions, so EC2 is blocked.

options.text: Nothing in EC2; S3 only if an IAM policy also allows it
options.why: Effective permissions require both the SCP and IAM policies to allow an action.

options.text: Use S3 automatically without any IAM policy
options.why: SCPs don't grant permissions; IAM must still allow S3.

explanation.answer: Effective permissions are the intersection of what the SCP allows and what IAM policies grant.
explanation.concept: SCPs are guardrails; IAM policies grant permissions within those guardrails.
explanation.examTip: Permission must be allowed by both the SCP and IAM.

stem: A company wants all IAM users to use passwords of at least 14 characters that include symbols.

options.text: Turn on Amazon GuardDuty
options.why: GuardDuty detects threats; it doesn't set password rules.

options.text: Enable AWS Shield
options.why: Shield protects against DDoS attacks, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: Ask users to choose strong passwords voluntarily
options.why: Voluntary rules aren't enforced, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: Set an IAM account password policy
options.why: An account password policy enforces length and complexity for IAM users.

explanation.answer: An IAM password policy sets requirements such as minimum length, character types and password expiration for IAM users.
explanation.concept: For workforce sign-in, many companies use IAM Identity Center with their identity provider's policies.
explanation.examTip: Enforce password rules for IAM users = account password policy.

references.title: Setting an account password policy for IAM users

stem: A security team wants to find S3 buckets, KMS keys and IAM roles that are shared with external accounts.

options.text: IAM Access Analyzer
options.why: Access Analyzer identifies resources shared with external principals.

options.text: AWS Health Dashboard
options.why: The Health Dashboard reports AWS service events.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure.

options.text: AWS Cost Explorer
options.why: Cost Explorer analyzes spending, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: IAM Access Analyzer uses logic-based reasoning to find resources that are accessible from outside your account or organization.
explanation.concept: It also helps validate policies and generate least-privilege policies from activity.
explanation.examTip: Who outside can reach my resources = IAM Access Analyzer.

stem: An auditor wants a list of all IAM users with the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA devices.

options.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake
options.why: CloudTrail records API activity, not a credential inventory.

options.text: The IAM credential report
options.why: The credential report lists users and the status of their credentials, including MFA.

options.text: The AWS Pricing Calculator
options.why: The Pricing Calculator estimates costs, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks
options.why: Cost checks are about spending, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

explanation.answer: The IAM credential report is a downloadable file listing all users and the status of passwords, access keys and MFA devices.
explanation.concept: Use it to find unused credentials and users without MFA.
explanation.examTip: Audit all users' credentials = IAM credential report.

stem: A startup asks how much IAM costs.

options.text: IAM costs a fee per user per month
options.why: IAM has no per-user fee, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: IAM charges per policy evaluated
options.why: Policy evaluations aren't billed, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

options.text: IAM is offered at no additional charge
options.why: You pay only for other AWS services your users access.

options.text: IAM is included only with paid support plans
options.why: IAM is available in every account, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: AWS IAM is a feature of your AWS account offered at no additional charge.
explanation.concept: Some related features, like certain IAM Access Analyzer checks, may have charges, but core IAM is free.
explanation.examTip: IAM = no additional charge.

stem: A company wants employees to use their existing corporate credentials to access the AWS console, without creating IAM users.

options.text: Resource tagging
options.why: Tags organize resources; they don't provide sign-in.

options.text: Root user sharing
options.why: Sharing the root user is insecure and not federation.

options.text: Access key rotation
options.why: Rotating keys doesn't remove the need for IAM users.

options.text: Identity federation
options.why: Federation lets users from an external identity provider access AWS with temporary credentials.

explanation.answer: Identity federation lets users sign in with an existing identity provider (for example using SAML 2.0) and assume roles in AWS.
explanation.concept: IAM Identity Center is the recommended way to set up workforce federation.
explanation.examTip: Use corporate logins for AWS = federation.

stem: A company wants to set up a secure multi-account environment quickly, with pre-configured guardrails and a landing zone.

options.text: AWS Control Tower
options.why: Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account landing zone with guardrails.

options.text: Amazon Detective
options.why: Detective investigates security findings.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
options.why: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations, not a landing zone.

options.text: AWS CloudShell
options.why: CloudShell is a browser-based shell, which isn't what this scenario needs.

explanation.answer: AWS Control Tower automates setting up a well-architected multi-account environment, using AWS Organizations and preventive and detective controls.
explanation.concept: Control Tower builds on Organizations, IAM Identity Center and AWS Config.
explanation.examTip: Quick secure multi-account setup = Control Tower.

stem: An auditor from a partner company needs temporary read-only access to resources in your AWS account.
prompt: What is the MOST secure approach?

options.text: Copy the data to a bucket the auditor can read publicly
options.why: Public access exposes data to everyone, so it doesn't fit this scenario.

options.text: Create a cross-account role with read-only permissions
options.why: Cross-account roles give temporary credentials without sharing long-term secrets.

options.text: Create an IAM user and send its access keys by chat
options.why: Long-term keys shared in chat are risky and hard to revoke.

options.text: Create an IAM user and email the password
options.why: Long-term credentials shared by email are risky.

explanation.answer: Cross-account IAM roles allow principals in another account to assume a role and get temporary credentials with limited permissions.
explanation.concept: Roles are preferred over long-term credentials for any temporary or third-party access.
explanation.examTip: Third-party temporary access = cross-account IAM role.

stem: A security team is writing IAM best practices for the company.
prompt: Which TWO practices should it include? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Require MFA for human users
options.why: MFA reduces the risk of compromised passwords.

options.text: Embed access keys in application source code
options.why: Hard-coded keys can leak through repositories.

options.text: Use the root user for daily administration
options.why: The root user should be used only for root-only tasks.

options.text: Grant broad permissions to avoid support tickets
options.why: Broad permissions violate least privilege.

options.text: Use temporary credentials through roles wherever possible
options.why: Temporary credentials expire automatically and reduce key exposure.

explanation.answer: IAM best practices include requiring MFA, using temporary credentials, applying least privilege and protecting the root user.
explanation.concept: Regularly review and remove unused users, roles and permissions.
explanation.examTip: Good: MFA, roles, least privilege. Bad: root use, hard-coded keys, broad access.

stem: An administrator wants to change the email address used to sign in as the root user.

options.text: Any IAM user in the Developers group
options.why: Group membership doesn't grant root-only abilities.

options.text: Any IAM user with S3 permissions
options.why: S3 permissions are unrelated to account settings.

options.text: The root user
options.why: Changing the root user email address is a root user task.

options.text: AWS Support, without verification
options.why: Support doesn't change root email addresses for you.

explanation.answer: Changing account settings such as the root user email and password requires root user credentials.
explanation.concept: Root-only tasks are a short list; everything else should use IAM identities.
explanation.examTip: Account email/name/root password = root user.

references.title: Tasks that require root user credentials

stem: A company wants to allow another AWS account to upload objects to one of its S3 buckets.
prompt: Which type of policy is attached directly to the bucket for this?

options.text: An identity-based policy on the company's IAM users
options.why: Identity-based policies on your users don't grant access to another account.

options.text: A password policy
options.why: Password policies set password rules, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: A service control policy
options.why: SCPs limit permissions; they don't grant access.

options.text: A resource-based policy (bucket policy)
options.why: Bucket policies are resource-based and can grant access to other accounts.

explanation.answer: Resource-based policies, such as S3 bucket policies, are attached to the resource and specify which principals can access it.
explanation.concept: Identity-based policies attach to users, groups or roles; resource-based policies attach to resources.
explanation.examTip: Policy on the bucket itself = resource-based (bucket) policy.

stem: A user's group policy allows s3:DeleteObject. Another policy attached to the same user explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject.
prompt: What happens when the user tries to delete an object?

options.text: The action is denied
options.why: An explicit deny always overrides an allow.

options.text: AWS asks the user which policy to apply
options.why: AWS evaluates policies automatically, so it doesn't solve the problem described here.

options.text: The newest policy wins
options.why: Policy age doesn't affect evaluation, which isn't what this scenario needs.

options.text: The action succeeds because the group allow is checked first
options.why: Explicit denies override any allows, so it doesn't meet this requirement.

explanation.answer: In IAM policy evaluation, an explicit deny overrides any allow. Without any allow, actions are denied by default.
explanation.concept: Order: explicit deny > explicit allow > implicit deny.
explanation.examTip: Explicit deny always wins.

stem: A company wants to apply stricter rules to its production accounts than to its sandbox accounts.
prompt: How should it structure AWS Organizations?

options.text: Create a separate organization for each account
options.why: Separate organizations lose central management.

options.text: Group accounts into organizational units (OUs) and attach policies per OU
options.why: OUs let you apply different policies to groups of accounts.

options.text: Use resource tags instead of accounts
options.why: Tags don't replace account-level guardrails.

options.text: Put all accounts in the root with one SCP
options.why: A single SCP can't apply different rules to different account groups.

explanation.answer: Organizational units group accounts so you can apply policies, like SCPs, to each group.
explanation.concept: Common OUs include Security, Infrastructure, Sandbox, and Workloads (Prod/Dev).
explanation.examTip: Different rules for groups of accounts = OUs + SCPs.
